what: Bindings to the Rust regex Crate Through the rure C API
title: Bindings to the Rust regex Crate Through the rure C API
text: (R-) rure provides high-performance regex operations using Rust regex crate (rure C API). rure docs: rure C API Rust’s regex library, guarantees linear time searching using finite automata. exchange, must give common regex features backreferences arbitrary lookaround. however include capturing groups, lazy matching, Unicode support word boundary assertions. matching semantics generally correspond Perl’s, “leftmost first.” Namely, match locations reported correspond first match found backtracking engine. Regular expressions must UTF-8 compliant determined using Rust’s str::from_utf8(). However, haystacks UTF-8 compliant conversion UTF-8 performed. Whether invalid UTF-8 matched depends regular expression - see ‘Text encoding’ section rure C API. Care must taken ensure expected behaviour.

title: Detect regex matches — re_detect
text: re_detect() re_set_detect(), logical vector length string. re_set_detect_each(), logical matrix one row per element string one column per pattern patterns.

title: Detect regex matches — re_detect
text: re_detect() returns logical vector TRUE element string matches pattern FALSE otherwise. re_set_detect() set patterns, returning TRUE patterns match. re_set_detect_each() returns logical matrix one row per element string one column per pattern patterns - showing patterns match string. NA values string result NA output. Patterns must valid UTF-8 work Rust's regex engine. non-UTF-8 patterns result error. string may contain arbitrary bytes ASCII compatible text useful, UTF-8 useful still. text encodings supported. re_detect() uses rure_shortest_match internally, faster short strings rure_is_match. two return identical results. set functions (re_set_detect() re_set_detect_each()) use rure_set_is_match, rure expose shortest-match variant sets.

title: Detect regex matches — re_detect
text: Patterns can match empty string ("*") return TRUE every element string, since zero-length match occurs start every string. Zero-length matches treated valid matches.

title: Detect regex matches — re_detect
code: fruit <- c("apple", "banana", "pear", "pineapple") re_detect(fruit, "a") #> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE re_detect(fruit, "a", start = 3L) #> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE re_detect(fruit, "^a|a$") #> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE re_detect(fruit, "b") #> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE re_detect(fruit, "[aeiou]") #> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE  re_set_detect(fruit, c("a", "e")) #> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE re_set_detect_each(fruit, c("a", "e"), start = 3L) #>       [,1]  [,2] #> [1,] FALSE  TRUE #> [2,]  TRUE FALSE #> [3,]  TRUE FALSE #> [4,]  TRUE  TRUE  # Zero-length matches count as matches re_detect(c("bear", "cat", ""), "a*") # all TRUE #> [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE  # Out-of-range start yields FALSE, even for patterns that match empty # strings. Here start = 5 lands on the empty suffix for "bear" (4 bytes), # but is out of range for "cat" (3 bytes) and "" (0 bytes). re_detect(c("bear", "cat", ""), "a*", start = 5L) # TRUE FALSE FALSE #> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE

text: re_find() returns offset locations first match. re_find_shortest() returns end offset location first match. end location place regex engine determined match exists, may occur end proper leftmost-first match. re_find_captures() returns offset locations first match well offset locations capture groups match. title: Find locations of the first regex match — re_find
text: Match positions use following convention: start 1-based byte position first byte match. end exclusive end offset (0-based), .e. position just past last byte match. match first byte "abc" start = 1, end = 1; match first two bytes start = 1, end = 2. end - start + 1 gives byte length match, substr(string, start, end) extracts matched substring (ASCII input). empty match end == start - 1. example, re_find("abc", "^") returns start = 1, end = 0. byte offsets, character offsets. strings containing multi-byte UTF-8 characters, start end correspond character positions, R's character-based string functions (substr(), substring()) correctly extract match. See details.

title: Argument type: regular expression pattern — re_pattern
text: rure uses Rust regex::bytes module. semantics differ PCRE, Oniguruma, base R's grep() several important ways: backtracking. engine finite automaton, backtracking matcher. runs time linear input length, backreferences ("\1", "\2", ...) look-around ("(?=...)", "(?!...)", "(?<=...)", "(?<!...)") supported. Attempting use raises error. Leftmost-first, leftmost-longest. Among matches starting position, engine prefers first branch alternation matches, longest overall match. example, "sam|samwise" matches "sam" "samwise", "samwise|sam" matches "samwise". Unicode default. "\\w", "\\d", "\\s", "." operate Unicode codepoints, bytes. "\\w" matches Unicode word character ("\\p{Alphabetic}" plus "\\p{M}", "\\d", "\\p{Pc}", "\\p{Join_Control}"), just "[-Za-z0-9_]". "." match newline unless s flag set. Byte-level matching available. Disabling Unicode "(?-u:...)" makes "." match single byte allows patterns otherwise split codepoints. Every search implicitly anchored "anywhere string". engine finds leftmost match anywhere haystack. Use "^" / "\\" "$" / "\\z" anchor whole string (see re_start start interacts anchors).

title: Argument type: regular expression pattern — re_pattern
text: rure wraps regex::bytes::Regex, &str-based regex::Regex. Two consequences: offsets byte offsets. Match positions start arguments bytes, characters. ASCII two coincide; multi-byte UTF-8 . Disabling Unicode unrestricted. Patterns like "(?-u:\\W)" "(?-u:\\xFF)", &str-based Regex type reject, accepted . default u flag , patterns behave codepoint-oriented. Byte-level behaviour surfaces Unicode explicitly disabled "(?-u:...)", examples show. pattern must valid UTF-8 error . string may contain arbitrary bytes, ASCII compatible text useful, UTF-8 useful still. text encodings supported.

Argument type: regular expression pattern — re_pattern
text: following PCRE features available, attempting use either raise error exhibit (possibly) unwanted behaviour. example, possessive quantifiers typically error, instead parsed nested quantifiers. Backreferences: \1, \2, \k<name> Look-ahead: (?=...), (?!...) Look-behind: (?<=...), (?<!...) Atomic groups: (?>...) Possessive quantifiers: x*+, x++, x?+ Conditionals: (?(cond)yes|) Recursion: (?0) Subroutine calls: (?&name) Callouts: (?C...) \\K (reset match start) \\G (match previous match end) \\R (newline sequence) \\X (extended grapheme cluster) need , use base R, stringi, stringr.

what: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
title: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
text: page describes start argument rure. start controls byte position regular expression engine begins searching. 1-based byte offset, matching R's usual indexing conventions. default, start = 1L, begins first byte. valid range 1 <= start <= nbytes(string) + 1. Values less 1 raise error; values greater range produce match (FALSE NA, depending function).

title: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
text: search start finds first match byte start. engine tries match pattern byte start; fails, tries byte start + 1; . start equivalent slicing string. engine receives full string may inspect bytes start evaluate anchors zero-width assertions. example, "\\b" position start inspects byte start - 1 decide whether word boundary exists .

title: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
text: search begins start moves forward: "^" "\\" assert start string (byte 1, newline multi-line mode). Since search move backwards, start = 1L can find match anchored "^" "\\". "$" "\\z" assert end string (byte nbytes(string) + 1, newline multi-line mode). Since search moves forward end, start <= nbytes(string) + 1 can find match anchored "$" "\\z". "\\b" asserts word boundary current position. start whose suffix contains word boundary can find match.

title: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
text: Let n = nbytes(string). valid range 1 <= start <= n + 1: start = 1L searches whole string. start = n searches final byte. start = n + 1L searches empty suffix end string. Patterns can match empty string (e.g. ".*", "$") match ; patterns require byte . start > n + 1L range. result FALSE detection location functions, NA extraction functions.

title: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
text: start byte offset, character offset. ASCII input two coincide; multi-byte UTF-8, start refers byte position, may fall middle multi-byte character. Use nbytes() (wrapper nchar(x, type = "bytes")) compute byte lengths.

title: Argument type: search start offset — re_start
code: # Whole string re_detect("abcabc", "a", start = 1L) # TRUE #> [1] TRUE  # Start at byte 4 (the second "a") re_detect("abcabc", "a", start = 4L) # TRUE  (matches the second a) #> [1] TRUE re_detect("abcabc", "b", start = 6L) # FALSE (only "c" remains) #> [1] FALSE  # `^` only matches at byte 1, so only start = 1 can find it. re_detect("abcabc", "^", start = 1L) # TRUE #> [1] TRUE re_detect("abcabc", "^", start = 2L) # FALSE #> [1] FALSE  # `$` matches at byte n + 1, so any start in 1..n+1 can find it. re_detect("abcabc", "$", start = 1L) # TRUE #> [1] TRUE re_detect("abcabc", "$", start = 7L) # TRUE #> [1] TRUE re_detect("abcabc", "$", start = 8L) # FALSE (out of range) #> [1] FALSE  # Empty suffix re_detect("abcabc", ".*", start = 7L) # TRUE #> [1] TRUE re_detect("abcabc", ".*", start = 8L) # FALSE (out of range) #> [1] FALSE  # Byte, not character: e-acute is 2 bytes, 1 character. nbytes("\u00e9") # 2 #> [1] 2 nchar("\u00e9") # 1 #> [1] 1 re_detect("\u00e9", ".", start = 1L) # TRUE #> [1] TRUE re_find("\u00e9", ".", start = 1L) # start=1, end=2 #>      start end #> [1,]     1   2

title: Find elements where a regex match occurs — re_where
text: re_where() returns indices elements string match pattern. re_set_where() set patterns, returning indices elements string patterns match. re_set_where_each() returns list integer vectors, list element corresponds pattern patterns filled indices elements string match corresponding pattern. matches result empty integer vector. re_set_where_each(), result list empty integer vectors. Patterns must valid UTF-8 work Rust's regex engine. non-UTF-8 patterns result error. string may contain arbitrary bytes ASCII compatible text useful, UTF-8 useful still. text encodings supported. re_where() uses rure_shortest_match internally, faster short strings rure_is_match. two return identical results. set functions (re_set_where(), re_set_where_each()) use rure_set_is_match, rure expose shortest-match variant sets.

title: Find elements where a regex match occurs — re_where
text: Patterns can match empty string ("*") return index every element string, since zero-length match occurs start every string. Zero-length matches treated valid matches.

title: Find elements where a regex match occurs — re_where
code: fruit <- c("apple", "banana", "pear", "pineapple") re_where(fruit, "a") #> [1] 1 2 3 4 re_where(fruit, "^a") #> [1] 1 re_where(fruit, "a$") #> [1] 2 re_where(fruit, "b") #> [1] 2 re_where(fruit, "[aeiou]") #> [1] 1 2 3 4  re_set_where(fruit, c("a", "e")) #> [1] 1 2 3 4 re_set_where_each(fruit, c("a", "e")) #> [[1]] #> [1] 1 2 3 4 #>  #> [[2]] #> [1] 1 3 4 #>   # Zero-length matches count as matches re_where(c("bear", "cat", ""), "a*") # all indexes #> [1] 1 2 3  # Out-of-range start yields FALSE, even for patterns that match empty # strings. Here start = 5 lands on the empty suffix for "bear" (4 bytes), # but is out of range for "cat" (3 bytes) and "" (0 bytes). re_where(c("bear", "cat", ""), "a*", start = 5L) # only 1L #> [1] 1

what: rure: Bindings to the 'Rust' 'regex' Crate Through the 'rure' C API — rure-package
title: rure: Bindings to the 'Rust' 'regex' Crate Through the 'rure' C API — rure-package
text: Provides bindings 'Rust' 'regex' crate 'rure' C API, giving access high-performance regular expression operations 'UTF-8' compliant patterns. 'regex' crate guarantees linear time searching using finite automata. exchange, include common regex features backreferences arbitrary lookaround. However, include capturing groups, lazy matching, 'Unicode' support word boundary assertions. Matching semantics generally correspond 'Perl', 'leftmost first'. Namely, match locations reported correspond first match found backtracking engine.
